Recall the standard identity:
  x² + xy + y² = (x+y)² – xy.

Thus, our equation (given as)
  x² + xy + y² = ((x+y)/3 + 1)³
can be rewritten using (1) as
  (3t)² – xy = (t + 1)³,
or more explicitly,
  9t² – xy = (t + 1)³.

Equation (4) can be solved for t; indeed,
  (2n + 1)² = 4n² + 4n + 1,
so that
  4t + 1 = 4n² + 4n + 1 ⟹ t = n² + n.

Returning to equation (3) and after some algebra it turns out that one may write
  (2x – 3t)² = [(t – 2)(2n + 1)]².
sentence-category-reason: Rewrites the prior equation into a squared form using algebra.

sentence: Recalling that t = n² + n we replace t and solve for x.

sentence:
In one case the algebra gives
  2x – 3(n² + n) = (n² + n – 2)(2n + 1)
which, after rearranging, yields
  x = n³ + 3n² – 1.
sentence-category-reason: Carries out the substitution and algebra to obtain one expression for x.

sentence:
In the opposite case we obtain
  x = –n³ + 3n + 1.
sentence-category-reason: Gives the resulting expression for x in the other sign case.

sentence: Since x + y = 3t and t = n² + n, one may solve for y.

sentence:
One readily finds that the two possibilities are
  (x, y) = (n³ + 3n² – 1, –n³ + 3n + 1)
or, by symmetry (since the original equation is symmetric in x and y),
  (x, y) = (–n³ + 3n + 1, n³ + 3n² – 1).
sentence-category-reason: Presents the resulting ordered pairs for (x, y), using symmetry.

sentence:
Thus, all solutions of the equation in integers are given by
  (x, y) = (n³ + 3n² – 1, –n³ + 3n + 1)  or  (x, y) = (–n³ + 3n + 1, n³ + 3n² – 1),
where n is any integer.
